name: Altium Designer
tagline: Commercial schematic capture and PCB layout suite for electronics engineers, with integrated supplier and manufacturing data.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A PCB design suite is not an app, it is a geometry kernel, a constraint solver, a design rule checker, a netlist engine, and thirty years of manufacturing output formats that fabs actually accept. An agent can produce something that draws schematic symbols on a canvas in an afternoon, and it will be useless the moment you need a push-and-shove router, differential pair length matching, or Gerber X2 that a fab will not reject. The part that looks like software is maybe five percent of the value; the rest is component libraries, verified footprints, supplier stock data, and the fact that your board house and your coworkers already speak Altium. Worse for the DIY case: the good open alternative already exists and is free, so writing your own is pure vanity. If you want to stop paying Altium, the honest move is KiCad, not a one-shot build.
coreLoopDIY: A local browser tool that renders Gerber and drill files as stacked layers and diffs BOM CSVs between board revisions, so you can sanity check fab packages without opening the paid suite.
requirements: Existing Gerber/drill exports and BOM CSVs from whatever EDA tool you actually use
A real EDA tool for the design work itself, KiCad being the obvious one
whatYouLose: Schematic capture, layout, and any kind of autorouting or interactive push-and-shove routing
Design rule checking, electrical rule checking, and signal integrity analysis
Verified component libraries with footprints, 3D models, and live supplier stock and pricing
Manufacturing outputs that fabs and assemblers accept without an argument
Multi-engineer collaboration, revision control on binary design data, and release management
moatNotes: The libraries and the fab-accepted output formats are the lock-in. The UI is just where you touch them.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a dropped board spin costs more than the license, and because the whole supply chain around a hardware project assumes the file formats and library data the paid suites emit. Teams pay for verified footprints they do not have to re-measure, for a DRC that catches the mistake before the panel ships, and for the ability to hand a release package to a contract manufacturer who will not email back asking what this is. Individuals mostly do not pay, they use KiCad, and that is the correct answer rather than a homegrown clone.
notes: A Gerber viewer is a weekend; a PCB design suite is not. The moat is verified component libraries plus output formats the entire fab and assembly chain already trusts.
prompt:
Build a local-only Gerber and BOM inspection tool. Do not attempt a PCB editor.

Stack, no substitutions: Vite + TypeScript + React, plain CSS, no backend, no accounts, no telemetry. Everything runs in the browser from a static build.

What it does:
1. Drag and drop a folder or zip of fab outputs. Parse Gerber RS-274X files and Excellon drill files client side. Write the parsers yourself or use a maintained library, but pin the version.
2. Render each layer onto a canvas with a layer list: toggle visibility, reorder, assign colors, set opacity. Support apertures, flashes, draws, arcs, and polygon fills. Mirror bottom-side layers on request.
3. Show board extents in mm and inches, a measuring tool between two clicked points, and a drill table grouped by hole size with counts.
4. Load two BOM CSVs and diff them: parts added, removed, quantity changed, reference designators changed. Column mapping is user-selectable since every tool exports a different header set. Show the diff as a sortable table and export it as CSV.
5. Persist layer colors and column mappings in localStorage. Nothing else is stored.

Explicitly out of scope: schematic capture, layout editing, autorouting, design rule checking, netlist handling, 3D view, supplier lookups, cloud sync. Do not stub these or add dead menu items.

Quality bar: a 6-layer board with 40k Gerber primitives must pan and zoom at 60fps. Use a single canvas with transform-based viewport, not DOM nodes per primitive.

Deliverables: working app, npm run dev and npm run build, a README stating what it cannot do, and sample fixture files under /fixtures with a test that parses them. No .env needed because there are no secrets.
